title: Envy of Heaven
logline: A palace called itself the Envy of Heaven. It was a finished palace for about eight years. Find out what it was, what happened to it, and put it back, using only what you can prove.
question: What did this building look like on the day it earned its name, and where did that go?

facts.claim: The palace inscription gives two dates, 1781 and 1791. Rice reads them as begun in Hyder Ali's time and completed under Tipu Sultan. The ASI board at the entrance gives 1778 to 1789. The palace stood inside Bangalore Fort.
facts.source: B. L. Rice, Epigraphia Carnatica IX (1905), Bangalore no. 7 and introduction p. 27; Mackenzie's survey of Bangalore, March 1791; the ASI board at the entrance, as recorded in Epocheye's palace research notes
facts.source_internal: B. L. Rice, Epigraphia Carnatica IX (1905), Bangalore no. 7 and introduction p. 27; Mackenzie's survey of Bangalore, March 1791, key 14; palace research file palace-dimensions.json (dates tiered disputed)

facts.claim: From its completion in 1791 to the death of Tipu Sultan in 1799 is about eight years.
facts.source: Worked out from the dates above: completed 1791, Tipu Sultan killed 1799

facts.claim: Bangalore Fort: a mud fort said to date from 1537 under Kempe Gowda I; rebuilt in stone in 1761, the first year of Hyder Ali's reign.
facts.source: B. L. Rice, Mysore Gazetteer (1897), vol. II p. 46

facts.claim: The Venkataramana temple in the fort was built under Chikka Devaraja Wadiyar and immediately adjoins the palace on the north-east. No year of building is recorded.
facts.source: Epigraphia Carnatica IX, Bangalore no. 118 and introduction p. 27

facts.claim: Teak framing and pillars, stone pillar bases and stone platform; the outer walls of mud.
facts.source: Epocheye's palace research notes; the ASI display board at the palace; B. L. Rice, Mysore Gazetteer (1897), vol. II p. 47
facts.source_internal: Palace research file palace-dimensions.json (materials, confirmed); ASI display board as recorded in photos_own/MANIFEST.md; Rice, Mysore Gazetteer (1897) II p. 47

facts.claim: Francis Buchanan, 10 May 1800: the palace "is composed of mud", yet "not without some degree of magnificence".
facts.source: Francis Buchanan, A Journey from Madras through the Countries of Mysore, Canara, and Malabar (1807), vol. 1 p. 45

facts.claim: A Persian inscription on a stone in the palace opens with the laying of the foundation and gives its two dates as phrases meaning Abode of Happiness and Envy of Heaven. The first is computed in a letter-number system devised by Tipu Sultan.
facts.source: B. L. Rice, Epigraphia Carnatica IX (1905), Bangalore no. 7, with his note on the Zar system; Rice, Mysore Gazetteer (1897) II p. 47 note

facts.claim: On 21 March 1791 an East India Company army under Cornwallis stormed Bangalore Fort through a breach beside the Delhi Gate.
facts.source: Mark Wilks, Historical Sketches of the South of India, vol. III (1817), pp. 127 to 129; the tablet at the breach

facts.claim: James Hunter, Lieutenant in the Royal Artillery, painted the north front of the palace in February 1792.
facts.source: Yale Center for British Art, B1974.12.1168, inscribed on the back "A View of Tippoos Palace at Bangalore Feby. 92"; title page of Picturesque Scenery in the Kingdom of Mysore (Orme, 1805)

facts.claim: Hunter's drawing of the palace entrance is also dated February 1792. The plates made after his views include the North Front, the West Front, and the Square and Entrance of the palace.
facts.source: British Library WD2893, "The Entrance of Tippoo's Palace, Bangalore Feby. 92"; plates of Picturesque Scenery in the Kingdom of Mysore (Orme, 1805)

facts.claim: James Hunter died at Vellore on 19 May 1792.
facts.source: His tomb inscription at Vellore

facts.claim: The plates after Hunter's views are dated 1804 and were published by Edward Orme in London as hand-coloured aquatints. The title page is dated 1805. Catalogues differ on the engraver of each plate.
facts.source: Title page and plates of Picturesque Scenery in the Kingdom of Mysore (Edward Orme, London, 1805)

facts.claim: The title page of Hunter's series says its plates are "from forty drawings taken on the spot by James Hunter, Lieutenant in the Royal Artillery; serving in a detachment from that corps under Marquis Cornwallis, in the war with Tippoo Sultan", and "engraved under the direction of Edward Orme, and published by him in Bond-Street, London".
facts.source: Title page of Picturesque Scenery in the Kingdom of Mysore (Edward Orme, London, 1805), read from the OCR text of the archive.org scan dli.calcutta.09945, not the page image; Tate Papers no. 19 (2013), which notes that the series claims views taken on the spot

facts.claim: Tipu Sultan was killed at Srirangapatna on 4 May 1799.
facts.source: B. L. Rice, Mysore Gazetteer (1897), vol. I pp. 414 to 415

facts.claim: Francis Buchanan's account of the palace is entered in his journal under 10 May 1800, at Bangalore.
facts.source: Francis Buchanan, A Journey from Madras through the Countries of Mysore, Canara, and Malabar (1807), vol. 1 p. 44

facts.claim: Buchanan, 10 May 1800: "On the upper story, it contains four halls, each comprising two balconies of state for the prince, and each balcony faces a different Cutchery, or court for giving audience. No persons, except a few trusty guards, were admitted into the hall with the Sultan: but at each end of the court was erected a balcony for the officers of the highest rank. The inferior officers occupied a hall under the balcony of the prince, open in front, and supported by columns as high as the roof of the upper story. The populace were admitted into the open court, in which there were fountains for cooling the air."
facts.source: Francis Buchanan, A Journey from Madras through the Countries of Mysore, Canara, and Malabar (1807), vol. 1 pp. 45 to 46

facts.claim: Buchanan, 10 May 1800: "At each end of the halls are private apartments, small, mean, and inconvenient. The public rooms are neatly painted, and ornamented with false gilding."
facts.source: Francis Buchanan, A Journey from Madras through the Countries of Mysore, Canara, and Malabar (1807), vol. 1 pp. 45 to 46

facts.claim: The British took over the administration of Mysore on 19 October 1831. "From 1831 the principal departments of the Administration were accommodated in the palace." They were there for some thirty-seven years.
facts.source: B. L. Rice, Mysore Gazetteer (1897), vol. I p. 429 and vol. II p. 47; Lewin Bowring, Eastern Experiences (1871), p. 13; Sankey (1873), p. 1

facts.claim: The engineer of the new offices gives among the reasons for building them "the fears of sudden collapse" of the old building, its inconvenience and the scattering of offices. The new Public Offices were occupied by April 1868.
facts.source: R. H. Sankey, Offices of the Mysore Government at Bangalore, Professional Papers on Indian Engineering, 2nd series, vol. II, no. LXIII (1873)

facts.claim: Tipu Sultan dismantled Bangalore Fort after the peace of 1792. It was rebuilt after 1799. From the 1860s an entrance was cut beside the Delhi Gate and roads were driven through the walls. A gateway and a short run of wall are what survive.
facts.source: Buchanan (1807), vol. 1 p. 44; B. L. Rice, Mysore Gazetteer (1897), vol. II pp. 46 to 47; Epocheye's research notes on Bangalore Fort
facts.source_internal: Buchanan (1807), vol. 1 p. 44; B. L. Rice, Mysore Gazetteer (1897), vol. II pp. 46 to 47; fort research file evidence.md; palace narration

facts.claim: Almost all of the painted decoration is gone. What is left are fragments, and they are faint.
facts.source: Palace narration (seed 105); own photographs 37 and 41, September 2026

facts.claim: In 1873 the engineer R. H. Sankey wrote of "the happy application of white-wash" to the block of the palace that still stood.
facts.source: R. H. Sankey, Offices of the Mysore Government at Bangalore, Professional Papers on Indian Engineering, 2nd series, vol. II, no. LXIII (1873), pp. 1 to 2

facts.claim: Today the timber is dark and polished, and faded floral painting survives in places on walls, ceilings and niches.
facts.source: Epocheye's palace research notes, and our own photographs of the palace, September 2026
facts.source_internal: Palace research file palace-measurements.md; own photographs 37 and 41, September 2026

facts.claim: Most of the palace Buchanan described is gone. Sankey, 1873: the main block "has now been cleared away", and "an adjoining block which housed the Treasury ... still stands". Rice, 1897: "The palace having partly fallen in the greater part was demolished."
facts.source: R. H. Sankey, Offices of the Mysore Government at Bangalore, Professional Papers on Indian Engineering, 2nd series, vol. II, no. LXIII (1873), pp. 1 to 2; B. L. Rice, Mysore Gazetteer (1897), vol. II p. 47

facts.claim: Buchanan, 10 May 1800: "The palace lately served the officers of a European regiment for quarters, while the privates were lodged in the corridor."
facts.source: Francis Buchanan, A Journey from Madras through the Countries of Mysore, Canara, and Malabar (1807), vol. 1 p. 46

facts.claim: Robert Home's engraving "Inside View of the Palace at Bangalore", published 1 February 1794, shows the timber colonnade.
facts.source: Robert Home, Select Views in Mysore (1794)
facts.source_internal: Robert Home, Select Views in Mysore (1794); palace research file palace-measurements.md

facts.claim: The hall's columns rise the full height of the building, as high as the roof of the upper storey.
facts.source: Buchanan (1807), vol. 1 p. 45; Epocheye's palace research notes
facts.source_internal: Buchanan (1807), vol. 1 p. 45; palace research file palace_viewpoints.json, viewpoint P6

facts.claim: The rule of this game and of our reconstructions: use only what the evidence supports, and label the rest.
facts.source: Epocheye method

facts.claim: The exterior colours in our model follow Hunter's watercolour of February 1792. Hunter painted a different front from the one modelled, so their placement here is our reconstruction. The 1804 plates of the palace are not on disk and were not used.
facts.source: Epocheye's palace research notes and the record of our reconstruction
facts.source_internal: Palace research files palace-measurements.md and TSP_period_assumptions.md; tools/play/AUDIT.md, sections 5 and 7

facts.claim: The painted walls of the upper hall in our model follow the idiom of the fragments that survive. What was painted in each room is not recorded.
facts.source: Epocheye's palace research notes: the style of the painting is recorded, what was on each wall is not
facts.source_internal: Palace research file palace-measurements.md, section 7.4; tools/play/AUDIT.md, section 4

facts.claim: For panels with nothing left, our model repeats the one recorded pattern across the upper floor and labels its extent as inferred. It leaves the ground floor plain. It never invents a pattern.
facts.source: The record of our reconstruction

facts.claim: We take the outlines of the plates as Hunter's, because his views were taken on the spot. We do not credit every colour of the plates to him, because they were engraved and hand-coloured for a London publisher twelve years after he died. That he served in the army that took the fort is, in our reading, no reason to doubt what his views show standing where.
facts.source: Our reading of Hunter's watercolour (1792) and the London plates (1804)
facts.source_internal: Our reading of F08, F08c, F08d and F08e

facts.claim: Read as a diagram, Buchanan's account arranges the court by height: the ruler on an upper balcony with a few guards, officers by rank, the people in the open court below. That the decoration was meant for the rooms where the ruler was seen is our inference from the same passage.
facts.source: Our reading of Buchanan's account (1807)
facts.source_internal: Our reading of F12 and F13

facts.claim: The offices kept the surviving block in use until 1868, and we think that use is a good part of why it was kept. No record says so.
facts.source: Our reading of the office records: Rice (1897), Bowring (1871) and Sankey (1873)
facts.source_internal: Our reading of F14, F15 and F19

facts.claim: Hunter's two dated views of the palace, of February 1792, are the oldest dated pictures of it that we know of. Robert Home's view was published on 1 February 1794 and the date he drew it is not recorded, so we do not call Hunter's the oldest pictures outright. We do not hold the 1804 plates of the palace.
facts.source: Our reading of Hunter's watercolour (1792), the London plates (1804) and Robert Home's views (1794)
facts.source_internal: Our reading of F08, F08b and F24; palace research file palace-measurements.md, section 0.3; tools/play/AUDIT.md, section 7

facts.claim: Most visitors photograph the front, call it nice and old, and leave.
facts.source: [SAMBIT: your gate observation. Keep or cut.]

facts.claim: When the painted decoration was lost. The rooms were painted in May 1800. Whitewash is recorded by 1873. No date between the two is recorded.
facts.source: Bounded by Buchanan (1807) and Sankey (1873)

facts.claim: Whether the palace was finished before or after the fort fell on 21 March 1791. A survey of March 1791 already marks a palace, and the inscription's second date marks the end of the painting. Nothing fixes the order.
facts.source: Mackenzie's survey of Bangalore, March 1791; Epigraphia Carnatica IX, Bangalore no. 7

facts.claim: What the palace was used for after 1800 and before 1831. No record of the palace itself has been found.
facts.source: No record found

facts.claim: The colours of anything Hunter did not draw and the building did not keep. The painted composition of each individual room is unrecorded.
facts.source: Epocheye's palace research notes: the painting of each room is not recorded
